aircraft.type: Czech Sport Aircraft Piper Sport (light-sport aircraft)

narrative:
On September 8, 2022, about 1626 Pacific daylight time, a Czech Sport Aircraft, Piper Sport, N126WK, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident in Santa Monica, California. The flight instructor and passenger were fatally injured. The light-sport airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Part 91 instructional flight.

The flight was an introductory flight lesson for the passenger with a flight school based at the Santa Monica Municipal Airport (SMO).

Automatic dependent surveillance-broadcast (ADS-B) data indicated that the airplane departed from runway 21 at 1551, then flew the runway heading and turned to the west after reaching the Pacific shoreline a few minutes later. The airplane continued to fly west along the coast, at altitudes varying between 600 and 2,775 ft mean sea level (msl). After performing a series of left 180° turns, the airplane reached Malibu. The airplane then turned inland around the Pointe Dume Peninsula, and then east along the coast toward Santa Monica. During the return leg, the airplane performed two 360° steep turn maneuvers, and by 1622, the airplane had joined the right downwind leg for runway 21 at the traffic pattern altitude of 1,200 ft msl.

By the time the airplane had reached the turn for the traffic pattern's base leg, it had climbed to 1,375 ft msl and began to descend, reaching 600 ft once it was established on final about 1.25 miles from the runway threshold.

Multiple witnesses observed the airplane land on runway 21, with one describing the landing as "hard." The witnesses stated that the airplane then began to aggressively pitch up and climb while the engine made a sound consistent with it going to full power. All the witnesses provided similar accounts of the airplane continuing to climb in a nose-up attitude before leveling off at the apex of the climb, about 100-200 ft agl, then spinning to the left, descending, and colliding with the ground.

A security video camera located on the southeast side of the airport, adjacent to the runway 21 threshold, and facing north, captured the final landing approach segment. The video showed the airplane descending over the runway threshold markings at an altitude of about 25 ft agl and then passing to the left and out of the camera's field of view. A second camera, similarly positioned but facing northwest, captured the other end of the runway threshold markings. As the airplane came into view, the main landing gear was already on the ground and the airplane then began to climb in a slightly nose-up attitude. Over the next three seconds, the airplane pitched up to an almost vertical attitude and climbed out of the camera's field of view. The shadow of the airplane on the runway surface indicated that it continued to climb for another two seconds before descending and striking the ground about 5 seconds later.

Audio recording of the airport's CTAF captured the airplane's radio transmissions during the landing approach. The flight instructor provided clear indications of the airplane's position as it flew in the traffic pattern, and the tower controller provided the pilot a clearance for "the option" during the landing approach. The flight instructor responded that it was to be a full-stop landing, and a few seconds later the audio captured him screaming, "let go, let go……. let go, let go, let go."

The airplane struck the ground in a nose-down attitude and came to rest at the intersection of taxiway B and B4, about 375 ft south of the runway 21 threshold.
probable_cause: The pilot's inability to maintain control of the airplane during the landing flare due to the passenger's excessive control inputs, which resulted in the airplane exceeding its critical angle of attack and entering an aerodynamic stall.
phase_of_flight: Landing flare/touchdown, followed by an abrupt go-around maneuver (defining event), initial climb, loss of control in flight, uncontrolled descent, and collision with terrain (non-CFIT)
weather: Visual meteorological conditions (VMC): clear skies, no ceiling, 10 miles visibility, wind 7 kt from 250°, temperature 32°C / dew point 17°C, altimeter 29.64 inHg. Weather was not a factor.
notes: NTSB final report (12 pages) fetched directly from data.ntsb.gov's report-generation API and text-extracted with PyMuPDF; narrative and probable_cause are verbatim from the 'History of Flight' and 'Probable Cause and Findings' sections. Original publish date July 10, 2024 (about 22 months after the accident); Investigation Class 3. Findings list (NTSB's own categorized findings, separate from the prose probable cause): Pitch control - Incorrect use/operation; Airspeed - Not attained/maintained; Angle of attack - Capability exceeded; Aircraft control - Passenger; Anxiety/panic - Passenger; Expectation/assumption - Instructor/check pilot. Important terminology note: the NTSB report consistently calls the second occupant the 'passenger,' not a 'student pilot' - he held no pilot certificate and the flight was an introductory/discovery flight (a gift from family, per the report), not formal flight training of an enrolled student. The report also notes he was seated in the left (pilot) seat and the instructor in the right (co-pilot) seat, and that the 'let go' transmissions were picked up on the passenger's microphone because he was inadvertently holding the push-to-talk switch on his control stick, which also blocked the instructor's own transmissions during the emergency. Names of the instructor and passenger (Christian West and Jackson Nazario) are not given anywhere in the NTSB report itself - they come from contemporaneous news coverage (Santa Monica Daily Press, ABC7, etc.), not the official record, consistent with how prior cases in this dataset (e.g. ANC18FA007) handle unnamed-in-report individuals. Exact accident coordinates (34.017882, -118.44801) are NTSB's own stated lat/lon, not derived or estimated by this research pass. Operator field: registered owner/operator is 'SANTA MONICA FLYERS INC'; the report's structured 'Operator' field itself just says 'On file' and 'Operating Certificate(s) Held: None' (it operated under Part 61/91 as a flight school, not a certificated Part 135/141 operation).

page.title: PiperSport (N126WK)
page.subtitle: Stall and spin after a go-around at Santa Monica Airport
page.datetime_text: September 8, 2022, 16:26 PDT · Santa Monica Municipal Airport (SMO)
page.summary: An introductory flight lesson at Santa Monica Flyers ended when a hard landing led the instructor to attempt a go-around. The airplane pitched up almost vertically, climbed, then stalled and spun to the left before striking the ground. Both the flight instructor and the passenger — who was taking his first flight, a gift from family, and held no pilot certificate — were killed. The investigation found the passenger was inadvertently pressing his microphone button while gripping the controls, which may have kept the instructor from being heard as he tried to recover.

page.narrative_excerpt:
Multiple witnesses observed the airplane land on runway 21, with one describing the landing as "hard." The witnesses stated that the airplane then began to aggressively pitch up and climb while the engine made a sound consistent with it going to full power. All the witnesses provided similar accounts of the airplane continuing to climb in a nose-up attitude before leveling off at the apex of the climb, about 100-200 ft agl, then spinning to the left, descending, and colliding with the ground.

contributing_factors: Hard landing leading to an abrupt go-around
Passenger's excessive aft control input during the go-around
Airplane exceeding its critical angle of attack and entering an aerodynamic stall
Passenger inadvertently holding the push-to-talk switch, which blocked the instructor's radio calls and may have delayed recognition of the emergency
Instructor's inability to regain control before ground impact
safety_takeaways: On introductory/discovery flights, agree explicitly on who holds the controls during the critical landing and go-around phases — don't assume a passenger will let go on command once control forces build up.

Anxious first-time flyers can grip the controls far harder than expected — the FAA's own guidance warns learners can be "incredibly strong" and react inappropriately under stress; brief this risk before every introductory flight, not just experienced-student flights.
A positive exchange of flight controls ("I have the flight controls," confirmed verbally) should be practiced and enforced on every flight with a non-pilot aboard, especially during a go-around.

Be aware that intercom/PTT design can let a panicking occupant's grip on the stick silence the pilot's own transmissions at the exact moment communication matters most — know your aircraft's intercom behavior.

A go-around after a hard landing is already a high-workload maneuver; with an unbriefed or startled passenger on the controls, be prepared to take over immediately and firmly rather than attempt to talk them off the controls first.
